A few days ago I [wrote](../2026-10-22-lfx-kernel-mentorship/index.qmd) that kernel
maintainers were much kinder than their reputation. This week a review of mine
included the word "NAK", followed by a homework assignment. I still stand by
what I wrote.

Between 22 and 26 October, Jonathan Cameron applied four more of my patches to the
`fixes-togreg` branch of [`iio.git`](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/jic23/iio.git/).
Three are in the Semtech SX9xxx capacitive proximity drivers (`sx9324`, `sx9360`
and `sx9500`). The fourth is in the Microchip `mcp3564` ADC driver. All four are
bug fixes with a `Fixes:` tag, and three of them are marked for stable kernels.
Andy Shevchenko reviewed three of the four, and each review changed the patch for
the better.

## sx9324: a table that was half as long as it should be

The SX9324 polls for new samples when it has no interrupt line. To decide how long
to sleep, the driver reads the scan period code from a register and uses it as an
index into a table:

```c
static int sx9324_wait_for_sample(struct sx_common_data *data)
{
	...
	val = FIELD_GET(SX9324_REG_GNRL_CTRL0_SCANPERIOD_MASK, val);

	msleep(sx9324_scan_period_table[val]);
	...
}
```

The `SCANPERIOD` field is 5 bits wide, so it has 32 possible codes. The table had
16 entries. It had been copied from the SX9310 driver, where the same field is only
4 bits wide. Every code from `0x10` to `0x1f` read past the end of the array, and
the chip's reset default is `0x16` (100 ms). In other words, a polled SX9324 with
the default configuration slept for whatever number happened to sit in memory
after the table.

![The scan period table before and after the fix. The old table covers only the
first 16 codes; the reset default, `0x16`, is one of the codes that read past its
end. The new values come from the period comments on the driver's existing
`sx9324_samp_freq_table[]`.](sx9324_table.png){#fig-sx9324}

The fix seemed simple: fill in all 32 periods, which the driver already documented
in the comments of its `sx9324_samp_freq_table[]`, and add a `static_assert()` so
the two tables can never disagree in length again. My v1 packed the 32 values into
three lines, as tightly as they would fit. Andy's reply was short:

> NAK to this hunk.\
> Homework:\
> read my comments regarding formatting such arrays in linux-iio@ mailing list\
> for last calendar year or so and summarize the idea.

That was my first NAK. To be honest it stung for a minute, and then I realised
it was one of the most useful replies I had received. Andy hadn't rewritten the
table for me. He told me where the answer was and trusted me to find it. I replied
within a few minutes to say I would do the homework.

I keep a local git mirror of the [linux-iio archive](https://lore.kernel.org/linux-iio/),
so the homework was a search through a year of Andy's reviews. The idea turned up
again and again, most clearly in a
[November 2025 review](https://lore.kernel.org/all/aRITLaJir-2IoclU@smile.fi.intel.com/)
of a new frequency driver:

> Make it power-of-two items per line, even with the comments to show
> the indexing, like\
> `810, 1620, 2430, 3240, 4050, 4860, 5670, 6480,	/* 0 - 7 */`

Once I saw it, the reason was obvious. This table is indexed by a register value,
so a reader has to be able to answer "what is entry `0x13`?" at a glance. With
eight entries per line and the code range in a comment, you can. With values
packed to fill the line, you have to count, and a typo can hide for years. The v2
looked like this:

```c
static const unsigned int sx9324_scan_period_table[] = {
	1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14, 18,			/* 0x00 - 0x07 */
	22, 26, 30, 34, 38, 42, 46, 50,			/* 0x08 - 0x0f */
	56, 62, 68, 74, 80, 90, 100, 200,		/* 0x10 - 0x17 */
	300, 400, 600, 800, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000,	/* 0x18 - 0x1f */
};

static_assert(ARRAY_SIZE(sx9324_scan_period_table) == ARRAY_SIZE(sx9324_samp_freq_table));
```

I also put the `static_assert()` on one line, as Andy suggested ("I would dare make
it a single line"), added the `Fixes:` tag and `Cc: stable`, and rebased on
`fixes-togreg`. Jonathan applied it a few hours after I sent it:

> Looks good and matches what Andy asked about.
>
> Applied to the fixes-togreg branch of iio.git.

Andy's review of v2 arrived later that day. It had one more nit ("5 bit wide"
should be "5-bit wide") and ended with:

> Haven't checked if this is part of any ABI. Otherwise LGTM,\
> Reviewed-by: Andy Shevchenko \<andriy.shevchenko@intel.com\>

Jonathan didn't ask me for a v3 to fix a hyphen. He replied "Tweaked and tagged."
and fixed it himself in his tree. Going from NAK to `Reviewed-by:` in two days,
with the maintainer cleaning up the last nit for me, felt like a real reward for
doing the homework properly.

## mcp3564: a NULL pointer behind a fallback

The MCP3564 driver identifies its chip by reading ID registers. If the ID is not
one it knows, for example on a newer part number, it falls back to the match data
from the device tree:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-mcp3564
%%| fig-cap: "The probe path in mcp3564_config(). The fallback was the only path that didn't check its result."
flowchart TD
    A[Read chip ID registers] --> B{Known ID?}
    B -- yes --> C[chip_info from the driver's table]
    B -- no --> D["spi_get_device_match_data()"]
    D --> E{NULL?}
    E -- "no: DT or id-table match" --> F[use chip_info]
    E -- "yes: bound via driver_override" --> G["before: oops on chip_info->have_vref<br/>after: return -ENODATA"]
```

`spi_get_device_match_data()` returns NULL when the device was bound with
`driver_override` and its name isn't in the driver's id table. The driver
dereferenced the result unconditionally, so that case ended in a kernel oops. The
fix is three lines:

```diff
 		adc->chip_info = spi_get_device_match_data(adc->spi);
+		if (!adc->chip_info)
+			return -ENODATA;
+
 		adc->have_vref = adc->chip_info->have_vref;
```

Andy gave it a `Reviewed-by:` on v1, together with a request and a thought about
the bigger picture:

> Fine, but I hope we will have something to land to actually do it differently
> for the drivers that don't want to use driver_override mechanism.
>
> Reviewed-by: Andy Shevchenko \<andriy.shevchenko@intel.com\>\
> Please, shrink the commit message to the point.

He was right on both counts. A NULL check in every driver is a stopgap, not a design.
And my v1 commit message took four paragraphs to say something that fits in one.
The v2 message is half as long:

> When the chip can't be identified from its ID registers, the driver
> falls back to spi_get_device_match_data() and dereferences the result
> unconditionally. That returns NULL for a device bound through
> driver_override whose name isn't in the id table, causing an oops.
>
> Return -ENODATA in that case.

That taught me to write the shortest message that still explains the bug. Jonathan
replied with a single word, "Applied", which is my favourite word on the list.

## sx9360: a frequency that always became zero

The SX9360 stores its scan period in two registers, `GNRL_CTRL1` and `GNRL_CTRL2`,
as an 11-bit count of ticks. One tick is 8192 cycles of the 4 MHz oscillator. So the
period for a frequency *f* is

$$
\text{period} = \frac{F_\text{OSC}}{8192 \cdot f}.
$$

The driver's write function had the fraction upside down, and it scaled the
micro-hertz part of the value wrongly:

```c
reg = val * 8192 / SX9360_FOSC_HZ + val2 * 8192 / (SX9360_FOSC_MHZ);
```

For any frequency the chip supports, `val * 8192 / 4000000` is 0 in integer
arithmetic. The `val2` term always produces a multiple of 2048, so it never reaches
the 11-bit period field, but it does spill into the bits of `GNRL_CTRL1` above it.
Above about 0.26 Hz of fractional part it also overflows an `int`. To make sure, I
replayed both formulas for every frequency the driver advertises:

![The scan period programmed for each requested frequency. After the fix, the
period follows FOSC / (8192 · f) across the whole 1 to 2047 tick range. Before the
fix, the period field is 0 for every request, and for most of them stray bits are
written to the upper part of `GNRL_CTRL1`.](sx9360_freq.png){#fig-sx9360}

The new code computes the period the right way up, rounds to the closest tick, and
rejects frequencies the chip can't represent. While I was there, I noticed the
advertised range didn't match the comments next to it either: 4 MHz / 8192 is
488.28125 Hz, not 448.28125 Hz, and the minimum and step were wrong too. Before sending v1,
I also checked in userspace that the default 102 ms period survived the round trip: 9.765625 Hz → period
50 → 9.765625 Hz.

Andy's review of v1 was a series of short, precise questions:

> `unsigned int period;`
>
> What's the units for period? Seconds?

> `u64 freq_uhz;`
>
> _uHz

> `freq_uhz = (u64)val * MICRO + val2;`
>
> Read what units.h has for units of Hz.

> Missing blank line. Always make guard()() to be standalone in the code.

None of these change what the code does, but each makes it easier to read. A
variable called `period` in a function full of hertz and oscillator cycles
*should* make a reader ask "in what?". `MICRO` is a plain number, while
`MICROHZ_PER_HZ` from `<linux/units.h>` says what it is converting. So v2 renamed
the variable to `period_ticks`, said in a comment what a tick is, switched to
`freq_uHz` and `MICROHZ_PER_HZ`, and gave `guard(mutex)` a line of its own:

```c
	freq_uHz = (u64)val * MICROHZ_PER_HZ + val2;
	if (!freq_uHz)
		return -EINVAL;

	/* The register holds the scan period in ticks of 8192 FOSC cycles. */
	period_ticks = DIV64_U64_ROUND_CLOSEST((u64)SX9360_FOSC_HZ * MICROHZ_PER_HZ,
					       freq_uHz * 8192);
	if (!period_ticks || period_ticks > SX9360_REG_GNRL_SCANPERIOD_MAX)
		return -EINVAL;

	buf = cpu_to_be16(period_ticks);

	guard(mutex)(&data->mutex);
```

Andy also suggested that "at some point" the frequency table should become a plain
array of ints. That is a cleanup rather than a fix, so I left it for a separate
patch and said so below the `---` line. Fifteen minutes after I sent v2, Jonathan
replied:

> Seems like you've addressed Andy's comments (except for the 'at some
> point' one which is fine to leave for now).
> Looks good to me, so rather than keep track of this one I'm
> going to speculatively apply it to the fixes-togreg branch of iio.git
> and mark it for stable.

"Rather than keep track of this one" is a small phrase, but it says a lot. A
maintainer has hundreds of threads to track, and a patch that clearly answers every
review comment is one he can take off his list straight away. Writing a precise
changelog is how I can make that easier for him.

## sx9500: reference counts that drift

The SX9500 driver keeps reference counts of who is using each channel and the
close/far interrupt. A channel is powered on when its count goes from 0 to 1, and
off when it drops back to 0. `sx9500_write_event_config()` incremented or
decremented these counts on *every* write to an event's `en` attribute, even when
the event was already in the requested state.

That lets the counts drift away from reality. Writing 0 to an event that is already
disabled takes the count to −1. A following write of 1 brings it back to 0, which is
not the 0 → 1 transition that turns the channel on. The event now reads as enabled,
but the channel and its interrupt are off. Because raw reads share `channel_users[]`,
a raw read can then wait forever for a conversion that never starts. Writing 1 twice
and then 0 does the opposite: the event reads as disabled but the channel stays on.

![`channel_users[]` for two write sequences. Before the fix (red), redundant writes
move the count, and the event state and channel power end up disagreeing. After the
fix (blue, dashed), a write that doesn't change state returns early.](sx9500_counts.png){#fig-sx9500}

The newer SX9xxx drivers share `sx_common_write_event_config()`, which already
returns early when the state doesn't change. The SX9500 predates that common code,
so the fix brings it in line:

```diff
 	mutex_lock(&data->mutex);

+	/* The user counts must only change when the state does. */
+	if (data->event_enabled[chan->channel] == state) {
+		ret = 0;
+		goto out_unlock;
+	}
+
 	if (state) {
```

I don't have SX9500 hardware, so I checked both write sequences with a userspace
model of the counting and said exactly that below the `---` line. This was the only
one of the four that went in as first sent. Jonathan's reply in full:

> Applied and marked for stable.
>
> thanks
>
> Jonathan

I hadn't added `Cc: stable` to this one. Jonathan decided it deserved a backport and
added the tag himself.

## What these reviews taught me

Looking back over the four threads, very few of the review comments were about
whether the code worked. They were about whether the *next* person could read it:

| Patch | Review comment | What I changed |
|---|---|---|
| sx9324 | Table formatting: NAK + homework | 8 entries per line with index comments |
| sx9324 | `static_assert()` on one line | Joined the line |
| sx9324 | "5 bit" → "5-bit" | Jonathan fixed it while applying |
| mcp3564 | "Shrink the commit message to the point" | Four paragraphs → two |
| sx9360 | Units for `period`? | `period_ticks` and a comment saying what a tick is |
| sx9360 | `_uHz`, use `units.h` | `freq_uHz`, `MICROHZ_PER_HZ` |
| sx9360 | `guard()()` must stand alone | Added a blank line |
| sx9360 | Table should be a plain int array | Deferred to a later cleanup, with agreement |

: The review comments on the four patches, and how each was addressed. {#tbl-review}

A few habits came out of this week:

- **When a reviewer points you at the archive, read the archive.** Andy's homework
  took me longer than rewriting the table myself would have. But now I know a
  rule he applies to every indexed table, and I won't need to be told again.
- **Units belong in names.** `period_ticks`, `freq_uHz` and `MICROHZ_PER_HZ` make
  the code document itself.
- **The changelog is part of the patch.** Each v2 listed every comment and who made
  it, and said what I hadn't done and why. That is what let Jonathan apply the sx9360
  fix fifteen minutes after it arrived.
- **Say what you tested.** All four patches say "Compile-tested only" under the `---`
  line, along with whatever checking I could do without the hardware. Maintainers
  can only judge the risk of a patch if you're honest about this.

on the list as I write this, a series that keeps the IRQ balanced across suspend
and resume, and a hysteresis fix for the `sx9310`, so this family of drivers
may get one more post.
